question: UMS stands for:
options: Unattended Machinery Space
Unit Monitoring Station
Underwater Machinery Survey
Universal Maintenance System
explanation: In UMS mode, alarms are relayed to the duty engineer and the bridge, and the engine room is unattended for set periods.

question: Before taking over an engine room watch, the incoming engineer should:
options: Only sign the log and read the previous watch's entries, then take over the machinery
Accept the watch without checking if relieving a senior engineer on the previous watch
Wait until the watch has started and then check things at the first round of the space
Check machinery status, standing and special orders, alarms, tank levels and work in hand
explanation: STCW Code section A-VIII/2 sets out what to check when taking over a watch.

question: The Chief Engineer's standing orders are:
options: Port state control reports on the deficiencies found at the last inspection of the ship
The crew roster for the engine department, with the watch list for each week
Purchase orders for spares, signed by the chief engineer and sent to the superintendent
Written instructions to watchkeeping engineers on how to run the engine room safely
explanation: Watchkeepers read and sign them, together with any night orders.

question: A Planned Maintenance System (PMS) schedules maintenance based on:
options: Running hours or calendar intervals, plus manufacturer and class requirements
The crew's spare time and the weather, so that the work is done when the ship is quiet
Only breakdowns, so that each job is planned after the machinery has failed in service
The voyage cargo and the ports of call, with maintenance only done alongside in port
explanation: PMS is part of the ISM Safety Management System and is checked during audits.

question: Condition-based maintenance uses:
options: Monitoring data such as vibration, oil analysis and temperatures to decide when to maintain
Maintenance only after failure, when the machinery has stopped or has been damaged
Fixed intervals only, taken from the maker's manual, whatever the condition of the machinery
Random inspections made by the duty engineer whenever there is time between the rounds
explanation: It can reduce unnecessary overhauls and find faults before they cause failures.

question: During bunkering, fuel tanks should normally not be filled above about:
options: 110% of capacity
100% of capacity
90% of capacity
50% of capacity
explanation: Space for expansion and good monitoring of soundings help prevent overflows and pollution.

question: The 'dead man' alarm in the engine room:
options: Raises an alarm if an engineer alone in the machinery space does not acknowledge in time
Stops the main engine if the engineer on watch does not reply to the bridge in time
Monitors the bilge level and starts the bilge pump when the high level alarm is reached
Detects fire in the machinery space and sounds the general alarm to the bridge and accommodation
explanation: It is used during UMS when an engineer attends an alarm alone.

question: STCW requirements for engine room watchkeeping are mainly found in:
options: The ISPS Code part B
SOLAS chapter V, which sets the requirements for the bridge watchkeeping arrangements
STCW Code section A-VIII/2
MARPOL Annex VI
explanation: It covers watch arrangements, taking over, performing and handing over the watch.

question: Fuel oil purifier gravity disc size is chosen based on:
options: Engine power, as the larger engines need a larger gravity disc in the purifier bowl
Fuel density at the separating temperature
The ship's draught
Ambient temperature only
explanation: The correct disc places the oil/water interface correctly in the bowl. Modern clarifier-type systems may not need gravity discs.

question: After a blackout, the first priority is to:
options: Shut down all generators and wait for the main engine to be restarted by the bridge
Restore power by starting and connecting a generator, while emergency power runs essential services
Leave the engine room and muster, until the cause of the blackout has been found by the bridge
Restart the main engine before anything else, so that the ship regains steering and speed
explanation: Inform the bridge, find the cause, restore auxiliaries in sequence and restart the main engine when it is safe.

question: A shipboard risk assessment combines:
options: The time the job takes with the number of engineers needed to carry it out safely
The number of crew on board with the hours of rest that remain for each of them
The likelihood of a hazard causing harm with how severe the harm would be
Only the cost of the job, compared with the cost of delaying the voyage by the repair
explanation: Control measures should reduce risk to an acceptable level before work starts.

question: Regular lubricating oil analysis can detect:
options: Fuel sulphur content, which is needed to select the correct cylinder oil for the engine
Sea water salinity
Exhaust gas NOx content
Wear metals, water, fuel dilution and contamination
explanation: Trends in results help predict bearing wear and other problems.

question: Critical spare parts on board should be:
options: Identified, stocked at the required minimum and checked in the inventory
Stored in the accommodation, close to the chief engineer's office, in a locked cupboard
Thrown away after inspection, once they have passed their shelf life in the store
Ordered only after a failure, because the stock levels are checked once a year
explanation: Critical equipment is identified under the ISM Code. Spares support safe operation.

question: When the bridge requests 'stand by engines' for port entry, the engine room should:
options: Reduce engine room staffing, so that the crew can rest before the manoeuvring watch
Stop all auxiliary machinery that is not needed, to save fuel while the ship is manoeuvring
Make sure enough generators are online, prepare the main engine and steering, and man the engine room
Switch to UMS mode, so that the engine room is left unattended during the manoeuvre
explanation: Test controls and confirm communication with the bridge before manoeuvring.

question: A management-level engineer's responsibilities typically include:
options: Steering the ship and keeping the navigational watch with the second mate when in port
Only standing watches in the engine room, with the work planned by the shore office
Only cleaning the engine room and painting the machinery, with the watch handed over to juniors
Planning maintenance and budgets, supervising the team and ensuring regulatory compliance
explanation: STCW management level means Chief and Second Engineer, with overall responsibility for the machinery.

question: The engine room log book is used to record:
options: Personal notes of the engineers on watch, which are kept in the control room safe
Machinery readings, operations and important events during each watch
Only the cargo plan and the stability figures for the voyage, as entered by the chief officer
Only the crew's overtime and the hours of rest, which are checked by the port state
explanation: It is a legal record and must be filled in accurately and on time.

question: The engineer on watch should call the chief engineer without delay when:
options: Never during the night, as the chief engineer must not be woken in the sleeping hours
Machinery damage or a serious fault occurs, or they are in any doubt
Every hour as routine, to report the readings taken on the engine room round
Only at the end of the watch, when the log book is signed and handed to the next engineer
explanation: Standing orders list the situations in which the chief engineer must be informed.

question: The engineer on watch must inform the bridge promptly when:
options: The ship's stores are delivered, or the lubricating oil is landed ashore by the supplier
A routine filter is changed with no effect on operation, as the standby filter is in use
A machinery fault may reduce speed, cause a shutdown or affect the steering
The engineers change cabins, or the engine room staff are changed at the end of a contract
explanation: Early warning allows the bridge to take navigational precautions.

question: A fuel oil purifier separates water and solids from the oil by:
options: Gravity in a settling tank only, where the water sinks to the bottom over some hours
Heating the oil to boiling point
Filtering through cloth
Centrifugal force in a rapidly rotating bowl
explanation: The heavier water and solids are thrown outwards and discharged separately from the clean oil.

question: Fuel oil settling tanks should be drained regularly to:
options: Increase the fuel temperature in the tank by returning hot fuel from the heater
Remove water and sludge that have settled at the bottom
Check the tank vent
Add more fuel
explanation: Settling is the first stage of fuel treatment before purification.

question: A permit-to-work system is typically used for:
options: Hot work, enclosed space entry, electrical isolation and work at height
Changing a light bulb in a cabin, or other routine jobs in the accommodation
Reading the logbook and the standing orders at the start of each watch of the engineers
Taking meals in the engine control room during a long watch at the manoeuvring station
explanation: Permits make sure hazards are identified, controls are in place and the work is authorised.

question: A toolbox talk before a job is held to:
options: Order spare parts for the job and check that they are in the stores before starting
Write up the logbook for the previous watch and hand over the keys to the next shift
Brief the team on the task, hazards, controls and each person's role
Count the tools and spare parts at the end of the job and report to the chief engineer
explanation: It is a short meeting at the work site and anyone can raise concerns.

question: Reporting near misses is important because:
options: It replaces risk assessment, so that fewer written procedures are needed for each job
It is required only after injuries, so that the accident report can be sent to the flag state
It is a way to blame individuals for unsafe acts, and so to improve discipline on board
It helps the ship and company learn and fix hazards before an accident happens
explanation: A good safety culture encourages open reporting without fear of blame.

question: Records of seafarers' hours of rest are kept mainly to:
options: Plan cargo operations
Show compliance with rest requirements and help manage fatigue
Calculate the ship's speed and the engine load from the hours worked by the crew
Record fuel consumption
explanation: Fatigue is a major factor in accidents; port state inspectors check these records.

question: A newly joined engineer should receive:
options: No training until the next port, where a trainer from the company comes on board
A watch alone on the first day without briefing
Familiarisation with the machinery, safety equipment and emergency duties before taking duties
Only the crew list and a copy of the standing orders, which are signed on the day of joining
explanation: Familiarisation is required by STCW and the company's safety management system.

question: When ordering spare parts, the engineer should give:
options: The ship's IMO number only, as the supplier already knows the equipment fitted on board
The maker's part number, drawing reference and the equipment's type and serial number
Only a description such as 'small valve for the pump', with the ship's name and port
The price expected for the part and the delivery date, as the supplier will find the rest
explanation: Accurate information avoids the wrong parts being delivered.

question: Closed-loop communication means that:
options: The receiver repeats the message back and the sender confirms it is correct
Radios are switched off during the job, so that no messages are heard by mistake
Messages are written down only, in the log book, and sent by internal telephone
Only the chief engineer speaks, and the others listen without giving any reply to the orders
explanation: It reduces misunderstandings, especially during manoeuvring and emergencies.

question: After a major overhaul of a diesel generator, it should be:
options: Run without lubrication for a few minutes, to bed in the new bearings and liner rings
Put on full load immediately, to bed in the new rings and bearings under working conditions
Left stopped until the next port, so that the yard can check the new bearings and rings
Run in gradually, with temperatures, pressures and leaks checked before full load
explanation: The maker's running-in programme should be followed.

question: In an emergency, the general order of priorities is:
options: The cargo first, then the ship and the environment, with the crew's safety at the end
The ship first, then the cargo, then the crew, since the owner bears the greatest loss
The schedule first, then the cargo and the ship, with safety of life as the last matter
Safety of life, then protection of the environment, then the ship and property
explanation: This order guides decisions in the company's emergency procedures.

question: When the bridge rings 'Finished With Engines' (FWE), it means:
options: The ship is about to manoeuvre, and the engines should be ready at short notice
The main engine is no longer required and may be shut down following the procedure
The engine must be started immediately, because the ship is about to leave the berth
The engine room must be evacuated and the doors closed, as the ship is on fire
explanation: The engine room then secures the main engine and adjusts auxiliary machinery for port.

question: In fuel reports, 'ROB' means:
options: Received On Bunkering
Rate Of Burning
Remaining On Board
Reserve Oil Balance
explanation: ROB figures for fuel, lube oil and water are reported regularly to the company.

question: If the relieving engineer is clearly not fit to take over the watch, the engineer on watch should:
options: Not hand over the watch and inform the chief engineer
Hand over and leave anyway, since the relieving engineer takes responsibility on arrival
Ask the bridge to take over the engine room
Stay on watch without telling anyone
explanation: STCW watchkeeping principles say the watch must not be handed over to someone unable to carry out their duties.

question: The difference between a purifier and a clarifier is that:
options: A purifier works without rotation, using gravity to separate the water, and a clarifier does not
A clarifier removes only water, while a purifier removes only the solid particles
There is no difference, since both remove water and solids by the same method
A purifier removes water and solids, while a clarifier removes mainly solids
explanation: A clarifier has no water outlet, and is often used after a purifier for extra solids removal.

question: The water seal in a purifier bowl is needed to:
options: Add water to the fuel to wash out the salts before it is passed to the settling tank
Lubricate the bowl spindle and the bearings with a thin film of water from the supply
Form the oil/water interface and stop oil escaping through the water outlet
Cool the bowl and the spindle by passing a flow of water over the bowl shell
explanation: The seal water is added each time before the oil feed starts.

question: Oil coming out of the purifier's water (heavy phase) outlet usually means:
options: The fuel is too clean, so the purifier has no solids to discharge from the bowl periphery
The water seal has been lost or the interface is in the wrong position
The purifier is working perfectly, since the water outlet always discharges some oil
The sludge tank is full, and the sludge has been forced back into the water outlet
explanation: Possible causes include a wrong gravity disc, too high a feed temperature or too high a throughput.

question: Heavy fuel oil is usually heated before purification to about:
explanation: Lower viscosity and a greater density difference between oil and water improve separation.

question: During bunkering, the engineers should:
options: Take tank soundings before and after, monitor rates and levels, and witness the drip sample
Fill all tanks to 100% as quickly as possible, to reduce the time spent alongside the barge
Only check the bunker delivery note at the end
Leave the operation to the barge crew, who measure and sample the fuel on behalf of the ship
explanation: Accurate measurement protects against short delivery and overflows.

question: Mixing a newly delivered fuel with fuel already in a tank should be avoided because:
options: It reduces the sulphur content
It always improves the fuel quality, since the lighter fuel dilutes the heavier one
The two fuels may be incompatible and form sludge
It is required by MARPOL
explanation: New bunkers are normally kept in separate tanks until the fuel analysis results are known.

question: Bunker samples are sent to a laboratory mainly to:
options: Test the bunker barge's engines
Calculate freight, which depends on the quantity and grade of fuel delivered to the ship
Check the ship's draught
Check that the fuel meets the ordered specification before it is used
explanation: The results also help set purifier temperatures and gravity discs and identify problems such as cat fines.

question: When calculating the quantity of bunkers received, measured volumes are corrected to:
options: 100 °C, the standard temperature used for heated residual fuels in the heating tanks
A standard temperature of 15 °C using volume correction factors and the fuel density
The temperature of the engine room, measured at the sounding pipe of the tank
The temperature of the sea water, taken at the sea chest of the ship on the day
explanation: Fuel expands when hot, so uncorrected volumes give misleading quantities.

question: An increase in the viscosity of main engine system oil may be caused by:
options: Oxidation or contamination with heavy fuel oil or insoluble material
Too much clean oil being added to the system, which raises the oil level in the sump
A lower engine load, which keeps the oil cooler and reduces the oxidation of the oil
Dilution with distillate fuel, which makes the oil thinner and the viscosity fall
explanation: A fall in viscosity often indicates fuel dilution.

question: Infrared thermography is useful in the engine room for finding:
options: The water content in fuel oil, from the surface temperature of the settling tank
The sulphur content of the exhaust gas, from the temperature of the funnel casing
Hot spots, such as loose connections in switchboards and overheating bearings
The salinity of the feed water, from the temperature difference across the boiler drum
explanation: It allows inspection of live equipment without contact.

question: Management of change (MoC) means that before changing equipment, procedures or organisation:
options: Only the cost is considered, and the change is made if it is cheaper than the old method
Only the crew is told after the change has been made, in the next safety meeting
Changes are made immediately without records, if the chief engineer gives an order
The risks of the change are assessed and the change is approved and communicated
explanation: Unplanned changes have caused many serious accidents.

question: Engine Room Resource Management (ERM) focuses on:
options: Engine design calculations, such as the sizing of the cooling water and lube oil systems
Teamwork, communication, situational awareness and leadership in the engine department
Ordering resources from suppliers and agents at the best price for the company
Reducing crew numbers by combining the duties of the engineers and the engine ratings
explanation: STCW includes ERM training for engineering officers.

question: Before the engine room is left unattended (UMS) for the night, the duty engineer should check that:
options: All alarms are switched off and the bilge pumps are stopped, to avoid false calls to the cabins
Tanks are filled, bilges are pumped, alarms and fire detection work and standby equipment is ready
The main engine is stopped and the generators are shut down, with the emergency set on
The fire pumps are isolated
explanation: Many companies use a UMS checklist that is signed in the log.

question: In preparation for a dry-docking, the engine department should:
options: Order no spare parts before arrival, since the yard will supply everything that is needed
Cancel all surveys and repair jobs, so that the dock time can be kept as short as possible
Prepare a detailed repair specification and plan the work with the shore and the shipyard
Wait until the ship is in dock to decide what to do, with the yard staff on board
explanation: Good planning reduces dock time and cost.

question: The emergency generator is commonly tested:
options: Only after a blackout, when the main supply has failed and the set starts automatically
Only at the annual survey, when the surveyor is on board to witness the test
Never at sea, only in port, when the surveyor can attend and the set can be run on load
Regularly, typically weekly, including start-up and periodic on-load tests
explanation: Tests confirm automatic starting, the changeover to the emergency switchboard and fuel supply.

question: The main difference between a main engine slowdown and a shutdown is that:
options: A slowdown reduces engine load for less serious faults, while a shutdown stops the engine
A shutdown is only an alarm shown on the panel, and the engine continues to run normally
There is no difference, since both reduce the speed of the engine in the same way
A slowdown stops the engine immediately
explanation: Typical shutdowns are overspeed and very low lubricating oil pressure.

question: Engine room ventilation is usually arranged to:
options: Supply enough combustion and cooling air and keep the space at a slight positive pressure
Stop all air flow when engines run, so that the heat is kept in and the space is warm
Supply air only to the accommodation, with the engine room receiving only the leakage air
Keep the engine room under strong vacuum, so that smells do not reach the accommodation
explanation: Too little air raises engine room temperatures and affects engine performance.

question: Large main engine cylinder head and main bearing studs are usually tightened with:
options: An impact wrench at any torque, until the machine stops by itself on the final nut
Hydraulic tightening tools at the pressure stated by the maker
By hand only, with a short spanner, until the studs are firm and the nuts will not turn
A hammer and a spanner, tightening the studs by feel until they stop turning
explanation: Correct stud tension prevents leaks and component failure.

question: The officer in charge of an engineering watch should not be given duties that:
options: Involve reading gauges
Are part of the watch routine, such as taking readings and making rounds of the space
Involve logbook entries
Interfere with the supervision of the machinery on watch
explanation: STCW principles require the watchkeeper to give full attention to the watch.

question: Lubricating oil samples for laboratory analysis should be taken:
options: From a new drum of oil, in order to compare it with the oil in the system
From the bottom of the sump tank when the engine is stopped and the oil has settled
From a running system at the same sampling point each time, after flushing the sample line
From the drip tray under the filter, which collects oil that is flowing at the bottom
explanation: Consistent sampling gives results that can be compared to show trends.

question: To improve the removal of catalytic fines in a fuel purifier, the throughput should be:
options: Varied randomly during the day so that the bowl does not become fouled by deposits
Reduced, ideally close to the engine's actual fuel consumption
Stopped completely while the fines settle, and then restarted at a higher throughput
Increased to the maximum rated capacity, so that all the fuel is cleaned at once
explanation: Longer residence time in the bowl gives better separation of small particles.

question: If a purifier's gravity disc is too large in diameter for the fuel being treated:
options: The bowl will not rotate
More water will remain in the cleaned oil but no oil is lost
The interface moves outwards and oil may escape through the water outlet
Separation improves greatly, since the interface is moved closer to the bowl periphery
explanation: A disc that is too small moves the interface inwards and leaves water in the cleaned oil.

question: SOLAS requires at least two fuel oil service tanks for each type of fuel, each able to supply the propulsion and generator plant for at least:
options: 8 hours at maximum continuous rating
3 days
1 hour at maximum continuous rating, so that the tank can be changed over at manoeuvring
24 hours
explanation: This allows one tank to be filled or cleaned while the other is in use.

question: Water content in main engine system oil above about what level should be investigated?
explanation: Water can come from coolers, condensation or purifier faults and leads to corrosion and bearing damage.

question: Under a Continuous Survey Machinery (CSM) scheme, the classification society:
options: Never surveys machinery, as the chief engineer certifies it at the end of each five years
Surveys only the main engine and the boilers, leaving the auxiliary machinery to the owner
Surveys all machinery only once at the end of 5 years
Surveys machinery items in rotation so every item is examined within the 5-year cycle
explanation: This spreads survey work over time and allows it to be done with routine maintenance.

question: Under some CSM schemes, certain machinery items may be examined by the chief engineer when:
options: The item is new and has been supplied with a maker's certificate for use on board
The flag state requests it by email
He is authorised by the classification society, with the survey later confirmed
The ship is in dry dock only, and the surveyor has not yet arrived on board to attend it
explanation: Records of the overhaul and findings must be kept for the surveyor.

question: Main engine safety shutdowns can often be overridden from the bridge in an emergency, except for:
options: Overspeed
High exhaust temperature
Low cooling water pressure
Oil mist slowdown
explanation: Overriding a shutdown accepts the risk of engine damage to keep the ship safe; overspeed protection always remains.

question: A main engine develops 10,000 kW with an SFOC of 175 g/kWh. Its fuel consumption per day is about:
options: 4.2 tonnes
42 tonnes
175 tonnes
17.5 tonnes

question: The spot test (blotter test) of a fuel oil checks for:
options: Flash point of the fuel, shown by the colour of the ring on the paper after heating
Sulphur content, shown by the colour of the spot on the filter paper after heating
Instability or incompatibility shown by asphaltene sludge on the filter paper
Water content of the fuel, shown by the size of the ring on the paper after heating
explanation: A uniform spot shows a stable fuel; a dark central ring shows sludge precipitation.

question: Under STCW, management-level certificates for chief and second engineers under Regulation III/2 are required on ships with main propulsion power of:
options: 3,000 kW or more
10,000 kW or more
750 kW or more only
500 kW or more
explanation: Regulation III/3 covers ships between 750 kW and 3,000 kW.

question: A high CCAI value for a residual fuel indicates:
options: Lower density and viscosity, which improve the atomisation of the fuel at the nozzle
Poorer ignition quality, with a risk of ignition delay and rough combustion
Better ignition quality, with a shorter delay and smoother combustion in the cylinders
Higher sulphur content, which causes cold corrosion in the cylinders of the engine
explanation: CCAI is calculated from density and viscosity; medium-speed engines are more sensitive to poor ignition quality.

question: Under ISO 8217, the limit for total sediment (aged) in residual marine fuels is:
options: 1.0% m/m, which is the limit for total sediment potential in distillate fuels
explanation: Higher sediment indicates an unstable fuel that may block filters and purifiers.

question: In UMS operation, if a machinery alarm is not acknowledged in the engine room within a set time, the alarm system will:
options: Extend the alarm to all engineers' cabins and public spaces
Cancel the alarm automatically, so that it does not disturb the sleeping engineers
Stop the main engine at once
Switch off the fire detection
explanation: The escalation makes sure someone responds if the duty engineer cannot.
